issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: Ahmad is a 40-year-old Middle Eastern man married to his high school sweetheart. He works as a paramedic and has dedicated much of his life to saving others. However, a traumatic event involving the death of one of his young patients has left him struggling with severe PTSD symptoms. The trauma occurred on a particularly busy shift when Ahmad was dispatched to assist in an accident that involved several pedestrians injured by a hit-and-run driver. Among those critically injured was a small child who succumbed to their injuries despite Ahmad’s best efforts. This event, vividly etched in his memory, has triggered profound distress and flashbacks whenever he encounters visible injuries or the antiseptic smell of hospitals. Since the incident, Ahmad has found himself avoiding work as much as possible due to these triggers. When forced to go on duty, he becomes overwhelmed by memories of that day, which feel completely real across all his senses. These intense recollections not only bring back the same terror he experienced then but also leave him feeling permanently changed for the worse and convinced that he failed in his duty to protect others. The weight of these negative appraisals has led Ahmad to suppress thoughts about the trauma by immersing himself in work or other tasks, often working excessive hours. This overworking is a desperate attempt to keep his mind occupied and avoid confronting the distressing memories, but it has only compounded his difficulties. His concentration at work has significantly deteriorated, making him more prone to startling easily when touched unexpectedly. He also consistently chooses seats based on how safe or protected he feels. One recent evening, Ahmad was called to a scene where another child had been injured in an accident. As soon as he arrived and saw the visible injuries of the victim, his mind immediately flooded with the memory of that fateful day. The antiseptic smell of the hospital only amplified these sensations, sending him into a state of panic and causing him to react with alarm when a colleague tried to console him. This incident was particularly traumatic because it reminded him not only of his perceived failure but also reinforced his belief that he could no longer rely on himself in critical situations. As a result, Ahmad has become increasingly isolated from his colleagues at work and often avoids going to the hospital altogether. When he does go, he finds himself struggling with concentration and becomes hyper-vigilant about potential triggers. Despite these efforts, the memories continue to surface unpredictably, especially when he is in environments reminiscent of the traumatic event, such as a bustling emergency room or an accident scene. These intrusive recollections lead him to feel even more anxious and further reinforce his negative appraisals that he has permanently changed for the worse and cannot rely on himself. The accumulation of these symptoms and experiences has significantly impacted Ahmad’s personal life as well. He is now distant from his wife, often cancelling plans or becoming irritable due to the overwhelming distress triggered by memories and work-related situations. His increasing isolation and inability to cope with daily triggers have finally pushed him to seek help. Ahmad is most afraid that he will never be able to return to his former self, believing deeply that the trauma has left an indelible mark on him. At the same time, he hopes for a way to regain control over his life, manage his symptoms effectively, and find a sense of peace amidst the constant reminders of the traumatic event. In summary, Ahmad’s PTSD is characterized by a complex interplay between his triggers, maladaptive strategies, perceptions of threat, memory intrusions, and negative appraisals. Each component feeds into and exacerbates the others, creating a self-perpetuating cycle that has significantly impacted both his professional life as a paramedic and his personal relationships.
